newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Spain Sept CPI to fall, but risks seen.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Spain Sept CPI to fall, but risks seen.

text.p: After a lower-than-expected rise in August inflation, the Spanish bond market is expecting a further steady decline in September consumer prices but analysts on Tuesday warned there are risks of rebound.

A Reuter poll of economists showed on average that September CPI, due on Friday, should rise 0.4 percent month-on-month and 3.6 percent year-on-year, compared with 0.3 percent and 3.7 percent in August.
"Any data around these values are going to be neutral. But for the market there is more downside than upside," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

Official sources have reiterated many times in recent months that inflation is set to decline and the latest producer price data show there is indeed scope. In June, Spanish PPI declined 1.2 percent year-on-year.
But now that many seem convinced that Spanish inflation is well on the way to reaching the 1997 Maastricht target, prices could prove themselves a tenacious beast to tame.

A week ago, a Bank of Spain bulletin said there was still room for inflation to improve. A more recent Treasury report wrote that "the recent trend in PPI led us to more favorable expectations for coming months."

But analysts are more cautious. "We won't break the three percent level before the end of the next year. It seems to me that inflation is very close to its floor," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
The most optimistic opinions are for a possible break of the three percent target sometime during the first half of 1997.
But that could fall short of the mark if German prices declined beyond the most recent 1.4 percent level.
The Maastricht Treaty requires that inflation not exceed the average of the three lowest European Union member countries by more than one-and-a-half points for participation in monetary union.
In August, the Spanish government raised taxes on cigarettes and alcohol to cover a surprise hole in the 1995 deficit.
But the effect of the hike was more moderate than expected in August. Some economists are now wondering if there could be any delayed rebound.

"We could see a rise in prices of drinks. Many shops were shut down for holidays in August - maybe they decided to raise their prices only in September," said Carmen Alcaide, economist at BBV in Madrid.
In addition to the latent effects of the tax rise, other analysts are worried about inflationary risks tied to the development of unit labour costs - which the Bank of Spain recently warned about.
"If I should mention one, I would say the most difficult Maastricht criteria for Spain to meet is inflation," said Carmen Nuzzo analyst at Salomon Brothers.
